Eastern Arnhem Land

Vacant since the resignation of independent Yiŋiya Mark Guyula in mid-August. He was first elected to the Legislative Assembly in 2016

The by-election will be held on Saturday 12 September

Rural northeastern seat in East Arnhem Land. Its largest community is Nhulunbuy and it also includes Ramingining and Milingimbi as well as Galiwin'ku on Elcho Island.

More than 60 per cent of people in Mulka are Indigenous. The Djambarrpuyngu and Yolŋu Matha languages are spoken by almost half of the population.

Mulka has been held by Mr Guyula since it was created ahead of the 2020 territory election. The seat it largely replaced, Nhulunbuy, was a safe Labor seat for decades before Guyula won it in 2016.

Profile

Mulka sits on the northeastern coast of the Northern Territory in East Arnhem Land. The seat's name is a Yolŋu word which means "dry area" but is also used to describe a diplomatic space. In the eastern end of the seat, the town of Nhulunbuy is the largest population centre in the electorate. Ramingining and Milingimbi are the largest communities in the western end of the seat. Mulka also takes in Elcho Island and the Wessel Islands.

As with many rural seats in the Northern Territory the majority of Mulka's residents are Indigenous. The largest industry in employment terms is bauxite mining.

Background

Mulka was first contested at the 2020 territory election, largely replacing the former seat of Nhulunbuy which had existed since the first assembly election in 1976. The Country Liberal Party won the seat at the first two territory elections, but in 1980 it was gained by the Labor Party and over time became one of the party's safest seats. It has been held by two of Labor's deputy leaders, including Syd Stirling between 1990 and 2008 who was deputy chief minister during Clare Martin's entire premiership from 2001 to 2007. He retired at the 2008 election and was succeeded by Lynne Walker who became deputy leader in 2015 under Michael Gunner.

While Labor won the 2016 election, Walker suffered a shock defeat to Yiŋiya Mark Guyula, a prominent campaigner for Treaty and a university lecturer in Yolŋu studies. Guyula won by just eight votes, benefitting from strong preference flows from CLP voters.

Walker recontested the 2020 election against Guyula in the new seat of Mulka. They were the only two candidates and Guyula won with 55 per cent of the vote. Labor did not contest the seat in 2024 and Guyula held it against the CLP, his only opposition, with over three quarters of the vote.

Retiring MP

Guyula is a Yolŋu man of the Djambarrpuynu clan and the Liya-Dhalinymirr people born in Barrnyinnur in Arnhem Land, and started learning English from the age of 10 when he began a western education at Shepherdson College on Elcho Island. While living in Nhulunbuy he trained as a plane mechanic. He later returned to Elcho Island for work and eventually trained to become the first Yolŋu licensed pilot for the region in 1983.

Prior to serving in parliament he was a cross-cultural educator working for many years as a Senior Lecturer at Charles Darwin University. Across his life he has campaigned for a Treaty between Indigenous and non-Indigenous people.

He stunningly defeated deputy Labor leader Lynne Walker in the 2016 Northern Territory election to become the first independent member for Nhulunbuy, and was comfortably re-elected twice.

In mid-August, eight days before the 10th anniversary of his first election victory, Guyula announced his resignation from parliament, saying that he had struggled to work with the CLP government.

Guyula accused the government of being "not willing to listen or form partnerships" and criticised laws that were "dehumanising, oppressing and destroying our communities and our people." He also said the Westminster system of government was failing Aboriginal communities and that he would continue his work within the Yolŋu community outside of parliament.

McGrath is a registered nurse and health researcher from Galiwin’ku, and was the first Yolŋu registered nurse. He was brought up in remote Indigenous communities, schooled in Canberra, and studied in Darwin. He was the 2021 NT Young Australian of the Year. The 35-year-old is a father of three daughters.

Blamey has lived in the Northern Territory for almost 20 years and in Eastern Arnhem for almost three. He previously worked in construction but now works in the human services sector. He has also worked in youth justice, policy, and most recently has been developing programs for the regions libraries.
